newsitem.title: UK: British Liberals accuse rivals of lies on tax, EMU.
newsitem.headline: British Liberals accuse rivals of lies on tax, EMU.

text.p: The leader of Britain's third political party on Tuesday accused its two bigger rivals of "a conspiracy against democracy" in refusing to say whether they favoured the country joining a single European currency.

Speaking to London-based journalists from foreign media, Liberal Democrat Paddy Ashdown also attacked the Conservative and Labour leaderships for pretending higher taxes could play no part in reducing Britain's spiralling national debt.

Ashdown, whose party is Britain's most pro-European, said its two rivals were preparing "the biggest...deceit ever perpetrated on the British electorate" in ducking the single currency issue ahead of the forthcoming general election.
"Their pretence to the electorate that this is a decision that they have not yet taken is a conspiracy against democracy," he told the Foreign Press Association.

Prime Minister John Major and Labour leader Tony Blair, their parties split on the single currency, have insisted it is too soon to say whether Britain should abandon the pound sterling if the "euro" is launched as planned in 1999.

Ashdown said there was a similar compact of silence on the part of the two largest parties over the fact that Britain's national debt had doubled in the six years that John Major has been Prime Minister.
The increase was costing taxpayers the equivalent of seven pence in the pound on income tax, Ashdown said.
The Conservatives did not mention this because they were responsible for it, Labour because it did not want to discuss the implications for higher taxation.
"This country has to face up to some of these facts, and we will not say, like the Tories and Labour, that we will never use taxation (to rein in government borrowing)," he said.
"It is a lie, a straightforward unvarnished lie."

Governmnent figures published on Tuesday showed Britain's public sector borrowed 4.53 billion pounds ($7.05 billion) in August to give cumulative borrowing of 13.37 billion pounds in the first five months of the current financial year.

Ashdown's party has 25 of the 651 members of the lower House of Commons and is standing at around 14 percent in the opinion polls with a general election due my next May. Labour has a lead of some 20 points over the ruling Conservatives in the polls. ($1=.6428 Pound)
